newsitem.title: FRANCE: GOLF-SCAHILL LEADS BUT CARTER STEALS THE SHOW.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-SCAHILL LEADS BUT CARTER STEALS THE SHOW.

text.p: Little-known New Zealander Stephen Scahill led the Cannes Open golf tournament after the first round on Thursday, but remarkable young Englishman David Carter stole the show.
On a day when a capricious breeze billowed up many a score, rookie Scahill's four-under-par 67 earned him a one-shot lead as only 15 out of the 150 players broke par.
But among them was Carter -- just over seven weeks after surviving a life-threatening virus and an emergency brain operation.
Carter began his comeback by capturing a share of second place with fellow Englishmen Paul Broadhurst and Stuart Cage and Dutchman Rolf Muntz.
Carter endured an operation to remove fluid from the brain after collapsing in his room two days before the start of the Dubai Desert Classic.
"Everything feels fine and I'm back in business," said Carter, who is still troubled by short term memory loss.
"I had to ask the caddie the names of my playing partners in the pro-am soon after they told me them because I tend to forget things from five minutes ago.
"But I got the thinking side of my game right, the thing that I was most worried I'd forgotten."
Carter picked up birdies at the 10th, 13th and 17th holes to share second place.
"I'm extremely happy because I didn't know what to expect coming back out on tour again," he said.
Leader Scahill, 27, reckoned: "Putting is my strongest suit." The London-based New Zealander holed three successive birdie putts between the 10-15ft mark from the fourth to move into contention.
He bogeyed twice before the turn and again on the 13th to inhibit his round but surged back with four back-nine birdies, including putts of 25ft and 20ft."

Cage's best finish so far was to lose a playoff to Sam Torrance in the 1995 Irish Open, and Muntz, too, has not had a victory yet, but Broadhurst has, including the 1989 Cannes Open at the nearby Cannes Mougins course.
With rounds taking up to five and a half hours, the final group of players finished in near darkness.
